title: Purpose of the tournament rulebook
body: The Bluthelden® tournament rulebook establishes clear definitions of game mechanics and the resulting rulings. It also regulates tournament operation, the correction of rules violations, and the handling of repeated violations through to deliberate violations (Cheating).

title: Scope: official tournaments, league games and online events
body: This rulebook is the reference for all Bluthelden® rules questions. Compliance is mandatory in official tournaments. An event that does not apply this rulebook, or applies only part of it, cannot be an official Bluthelden® tournament or be sanctioned for earning Organized Play points.

title: Objectives and victory conditions
body:
Normal victory conditions
The game ends when one of the following conditions is met, as a Gamestate Check (section 4.10):
1. A Sovereign has 0 life points. The player controlling that Sovereign loses; their opponent wins.
2. A player must draw a card, but the deck they must draw from (Spell Deck or Pool Deck) is empty. That player loses; their opponent wins.
If either condition occurs for both players simultaneously, the game is a draw.

Other victory conditions
An alternative victory condition stated on a card applies when its condition is fulfilled and it has resolved through the Reaction Chain.
The game is also a draw if an uninterruptible sequence of mandatory effects makes normal continuation impossible (an infinite loop).

title: Card use and tournament legality
body:
Cards are tournament-legal only if the following requirements are met:

- Only original Bluthelden cards may be used.
- Digital cards are allowed only on officially sanctioned Bluthelden® platforms.
- Proxies are not allowed in official tournaments. Tournament management may provide replacement cards in exceptional cases.
- Cards in the Spell Deck or Pool Deck must not be distinguishable face down because of wear, damage or any other distinguishing feature.
- Cards with backs other than the standard Leros back require opaque sleeves with indistinguishable backs. This requirement applies to cards that can be part of the Spell Deck or Pool Deck.
- When sleeves are used, the same sleeves must be used for both decks.

title: Anatomy of a Bluthelden card
body:
Cards have a front with game information and a back that generally has no game information. The front is the side with the play cost, name and card type. Double-sided Sovereigns are an exception: choose one side for the deck and keep that choice throughout the tournament.

Every card contains:

1. Its name, centred at the top of the front.
2. Its card type directly below the name, possibly including Mythic or Epic.
3. Rules text describing its effects and abilities. If no game-relevant text exists, italic flavour text appears instead.
4. Rarity at the bottom left: K, N, L or F.
5. Set and language information.
6. A copyright notice.
7. The artist's name.

Other information depends on card type (section [2.2.3](#/en/rules/2.2.3)).

The background colour of the name and text boxes determines colour identity: White, Black, Orange, Green, Blue, Purple, Brown, Red or Grey (Equilibra).

title: Card types
body:
A card's type appears below its name. A card with multiple types has all attributes of those types. If those types have different timing restrictions, use the timing that permits the most opportunities to play it.

Cards fall into two categories:

1. Permanents remain on the battlefield after being played. They require a slot or a defined position. If no such position is available, they cannot enter play and go to the Graveyard instead. Playing a permanent is called summoning (section 4.1).
2. Non-permanents go directly to the Graveyard after resolving. They do not require a battlefield slot. Playing a non-permanent is called casting (section 4.1).

The defined card types are:

- **A) Sovereigns**
- **B) Runes**
- **C) Resources**
- **D) Characters**
- **E) Training**
- **F) Artifacts**
- **G) Rituals**
- **H) Spells**
- **I) Tokens**

### A) Sovereigns

A Sovereign has life points at the top left and additional costs for other colours along the left edge of its artwork. Each deck must contain exactly one Sovereign, placed in the Sovereign slot in the Government Zone at the start of the game. It belongs to neither the Spell Deck nor the Pool Deck, but counts towards total deck size.

#### Deckbuilding restriction imposed by the Sovereign

Its colour limits the Pool Deck to cards of that colour and Grey (Equilibra) cards.

### B) Runes

Runes have no additional icons and count as both Resource and Rune cards. Each deck contains exactly one Rune, placed in the Rune slot in the Government Zone at the start of the game. It belongs to neither deck but counts towards total deck size.

## Permanents

### C) Resources

Resources also have Pool and Binding icons and a level. A player may put only one Resource into play per round, whether played from hand or found using the Rune's ability. Each Lane has one Resource slot in the Safety Zone. Only level 1 Resources may be put in an empty Resource slot.

#### Playing Resources

A Resource above level 1 must be played on a Resource exactly one level lower. The lower-level Resource goes to the Graveyard as a result. Playing a Resource from hand is a special action and does not use the Reaction Chain (section 4.6).

A Resource opens its Lane for its player. Characters and permanents can be placed on that player's side of a Lane only if the Lane contains a Resource (section 2.3.1).

### D) Characters

Characters have an ASP play cost, level icon, optional Binding and Pool icons, Resistance, Initiative and a POW/HP box.

#### Playing Characters

They may normally be placed only in unoccupied Character slots. A Character can be played from hand only if its level does not exceed the highest level among its controller's Resources in play. This also applies when the Rune puts a Character directly into play from the Pool Deck.

#### Character abilities

Regardless of its specific text, every Character can Move, Block and Attack when in an appropriate slot. A Character with an INI icon has one action per round.

#### Character values

Printed RES, INI and POW/HP are base values (section 4.9).

#### Special type: Advisor

Advisor is a special Character type with no INI or POW/HP values. An Advisor can be placed only in an Advisor slot. All other Character restrictions still apply. An Advisor cannot take damage or have damage redirected to it.

### E) Training

Trainings have an ASP cost, a Fundamental or Martial type in the name box, and optionally Spellpower.

#### Playing Training

A Training can enter the battlefield only if it can attach to another permanent. Choose that permanent as a target when playing the Training (sections 4.1 and 6.1). The target must be in play both when the Training is played and when it resolves.

If the Training has Spellpower and its target has RES, compare them when the Training resolves or enters play. If Spellpower is at least RES, attach the Training. Otherwise it goes to the Graveyard without effect. Once successfully attached, it stays attached even if the trained card's RES later exceeds its Spellpower.

#### Additional rules for Training

The attached permanent is trained; references such as “trained Character” refer to that permanent. If it leaves play, the Training goes to the Graveyard (section 4.10).

### F) Artifacts

Artifacts have an ASP cost and may have Spellpower.

#### Playing Artifacts

They are placed in the permanent area, which can hold any number of permanents.

### G) Rituals

Rituals have an ASP cost and may have Spellpower. They are permanents placed in the permanent area, which can hold any number of permanents.

### H) Spells

Spells have an ASP cost and may have Spellpower and other subtypes. The types include Spell and Miracle; every Miracle also counts as a Spell. Spells are non-permanents and go to the Graveyard after resolving. Playing a Spell is called casting.

### I) Tokens

Tokens are permanents created by game effects. Their characteristics are defined by the creating effect. They may have one or more additional card types, such as Training or Artifact. They can be placed only if the requirements of their other types or characteristics are met. Tokens normally have no ASP cost; in that case their ASP cost is 0. A token Character with no level is treated as level 1.

Tokens exist only in play. A token that changes zones ceases to exist as soon as it is in a zone outside play, such as the Banished area, Graveyard or hand, and cannot return from there.

title: Battlefield and zones
body:
The physical battlefield comprises all zones and positions of every player. Each player owns and controls their own half and its slots. A card may be physically on the other side without changing control of that zone or slot.
Each player's battlefield is divided into Government Zone, Safety Zone and Combat Zone. These are the active zones, the battlefield in rules terms (section 4.8.1).
Only in active zones can cards be placed. Placing means taking a specific position within an active zone, regardless of the game process causing it. Each placed card normally occupies exactly one slot from the moment it is placed until it leaves. No further card may be placed in an occupied slot unless a rule or card text permits it.
Four additional positions do not belong to a zone: Banished area, Graveyard, Pool Deck position and Spell Deck position. These are inactive areas (section 4.8.2).
The Reaction Chain, where played cards and effects are placed, and the hand are part of the game but not the battlefield. They are abstract game areas (section 4.8.3).

title: Lanes
body: The Safety and Combat Zones are divided into three vertical Lanes. Each Lane includes part of both players' Safety and Combat Zones. The Combat Zone positions within a Lane are called its War Zone.

title: Combat Zone and War Zones
body: The Combat Zone is between the players. It contains three War Zones, one per Lane. Each player has six Character positions in total, two per War Zone. A War Zone consists of both players' Front Rows in that Lane, above their Back Rows.

title: Safety Zones
body:
Each player has a Safety Zone behind the Combat Zone, divided into three Lane sections. It can hold nine Characters and three Resources in total: three Characters and one Resource per Lane.
Each Lane's Safety Zone comprises a Back Row (two Character slots directly below the War Zone) and a Binding slot (one Character slot below the Back Row, left of the Resource slot).

body: Each player's Government Zone is below their Safety Zone. It contains a Sovereign slot, a Rune slot, an Advisor slot and any number of positions for permanents that cannot be placed in the Safety or Combat Zone.

title: Building a Bluthelden deck
body:
The complete deck consists of the Spell Deck, Pool Deck, Sovereign and Rune. The Sovereign determines which Pool Deck cards are permitted and which cards are excluded from the deck.

Pool Deck
Only cards with a Pool icon may be included. They must match the Sovereign's colour or be Grey (Equilibra). Minimum and maximum sizes depend on the tournament format (chapter 11).

Spell Deck
Only cards with an ASP cost and not excluded by the Sovereign may be included. Size limits depend on the format (chapter 11).

Copy limits
The total number of same-name cards across both decks is limited by rarity:
- F — Fabulous: 1 copy.
- L — Legendary: 2 copies.
- N — Noted: 3 copies.
- K — Known: 4 copies.
Cards banned or restricted differently from their rarity are listed in the format's Banned & Restricted list.

title: Sequence of play
body:
A round consists of the shared Start Phase, the Main Phase of the player with Initiative, the Main Phase of the player without Initiative, the Combat Phase and the End Phase. The following sections explain the steps, Reaction Chain and priority system.

At the start of the game, place the Sovereign and Rune in their slots. Both players draw six cards from their Spell Deck. Determine a winner by a random method such as a die roll or coin toss. That player chooses who initially receives Initiative. Mulligan decisions follow, then the first round begins at step 2, Draw Cards. Skip step 1, Beginning of the Round; no beginning-of-round effects trigger in the first round.

Mulligan
Once per player, set aside any number of cards from the starting hand face down, draw the same number from the Spell Deck, then shuffle the set-aside cards back into the Spell Deck. The player with Initiative makes their mulligan decision first, followed by the other player.

title: Start Phase
body:
The Start Phase has three steps:
1. Beginning of the round.
2. Draw cards.
3. Determine the player with Initiative (INI Check).
No player receives priority in any of these steps; neither hand cards nor abilities can be played.

Step 1: Unturn all cards first. Then put beginning-of-round triggers on the Reaction Chain and resolve them without allowing responses. If multiple effects trigger simultaneously, put the Initiative player's effects on first, then the other player's effects, and resolve them.

Step 2: Each player draws according to their hand size:
- Three or more cards in hand: draw one from either the Spell Deck or Pool Deck.
- Two or fewer cards: draw two from any combination of the Spell Deck and Pool Deck.
Players draw in Initiative order and announce which deck they are drawing from. Once both have drawn, proceed to step 3.

Step 3: Identify the Character with the highest INI. Its controller receives Initiative. On a tie, the previous Initiative player keeps it. If no Character has INI greater than 0, treat this as a tie and apply the tie rule (section 3.1.4). Proceed to Main Phase 1.

title: Main Phase 1: player with Initiative
body:
This is the turn of the player with Initiative. Put “at the beginning of your turn” abilities on the Reaction Chain first, followed by “at the beginning of your opponent's turn” abilities.
The Initiative player may play any type of card from hand and activate abilities in any order. They may also use the special actions Play a Resource and Move (section 4.6).
The other player may activate abilities, but may not play cards from hand or use those two special actions.
When both players pass with an empty Reaction Chain, proceed to Main Phase 2.

title: Combat Phase
body:
Neither player may play cards from hand during this phase. Each Character in play has one action per round. If not already spent, it may use that action to Attack or Move as the acting Character, or to Block in reaction as a non-acting Character. Each of these uses an action for the round.

Step 1 — Determine the acting Character and active Lane
Find the highest-INI Character in an unresolved Lane that has at least one action remaining, has not yet been the acting Character and has INI greater than 0. It becomes the acting Character and its Lane becomes the active Lane.

Step 2 — Choose an action
The acting Character's controller receives priority. After both players pass, choose:
a) Attack: consumes an action.
b) Move: consumes an action.
c) Do nothing: does not consume an action.

An Attack requires the acting Character to be in the active Lane's War Zone, unturned, with an action remaining and INI greater than 0, and not to have entered the battlefield during this Combat Phase.

Resolving an attack
Turn the attacking Character; it is now attacking. Attacks normally attack the opposing Sovereign. The acting Character's controller receives priority before blockers are chosen. When both players pass, the defending player may choose one blocker for each attack action. Turn each blocker and spend its action; that attack is blocked.
The acting Character's controller receives priority again. When both pass, combat damage is dealt: attacker and blocker simultaneously deal damage equal to their POW to each other, provided both are still in the same War Zone. An unblocked attacker deals its damage to the defending Sovereign, provided it remains in the same War Zone. The acting Character's controller receives priority again; when both pass, proceed to step 3.

Blocking requires a Character in the same War Zone as the attacker, unturned, with at least one action remaining for this combat. Blocking is voluntary. Effects that prohibit blocking prevent only the choice of this reaction; they do not stop another effect from making an object a blocking defender.

Step 3 — Find the next acting Character
In the active Lane, find the highest-INI Character with an action remaining that is unturned, has not yet been the acting Character and has INI greater than 0. It becomes the acting Character; repeat step 2. Continue until no Character in the Lane can act, then mark the Lane resolved and return to step 1.
Continue until all Lanes are resolved. A Character placed in an already resolved Lane does not reopen it and cannot become the acting Character.

Initiative ties
If eligible Characters controlled by different players tie, the Character controlled by the player holding Initiative from the last INI Check acts first. If tied Characters share a controller, that player chooses which acts first.

Step 4 — End of combat
Once every Lane is resolved, trigger all end-of-combat abilities. Characters in a War Zone at the end of combat that performed a combat action (Attack or Block) count as having survived until the end of the round. The Initiative player receives priority. When both pass, perform an INI Check for the end of the round: the controller of the highest-INI Character receives Initiative. Proceed to the End Phase.

Neither player may play cards from hand during this phase. Each Character in play has one action per round. If not already spent, it may use that action to Attack or Move as the acting Character, or to Block in reaction as a non-acting Character. Each of these uses an action for the round.

Step 1 — Determine the acting Character and active Lane Find the highest-INI Character in an unresolved Lane that has at least one action remaining, has not yet been the acting Character and has INI greater than 0. It becomes the acting Character and its Lane becomes the active Lane.

Step 2 — Choose an action The acting Character's controller receives priority. After both players pass, choose: a) Attack: consumes an action. b) Move: consumes an action. c) Do nothing: does not consume an action.

An Attack requires the acting Character to be in the active Lane's War Zone, unturned, with an action remaining and INI greater than 0, and not to have entered the battlefield during this Combat Phase.

Resolving an attack Turn the attacking Character; it is now attacking. Attacks normally attack the opposing Sovereign. The acting Character's controller receives priority before blockers are chosen. When both players pass, the defending player may choose one blocker for each attack action. Turn each blocker and spend its action; that attack is blocked. The acting Character's controller receives priority again. When both pass, combat damage is dealt: attacker and blocker simultaneously deal damage equal to their POW to each other, provided both are still in the same War Zone. An unblocked attacker deals its damage to the defending Sovereign, provided it remains in the same War Zone. The acting Character's controller receives priority again; when both pass, proceed to step 3.

Blocking requires a Character in the same War Zone as the attacker, unturned, with at least one action remaining for this combat. Blocking is voluntary. Effects that prohibit blocking prevent only the choice of this reaction; they do not stop another effect from making an object a blocking defender.

Step 3 — Find the next acting Character In the active Lane, find the highest-INI Character with an action remaining that is unturned, has not yet been the acting Character and has INI greater than 0. It becomes the acting Character; repeat step 2. Continue until no Character in the Lane can act, then mark the Lane resolved and return to step 1. Continue until all Lanes are resolved. A Character placed in an already resolved Lane does not reopen it and cannot become the acting Character.

Characters in a War Zone at the end of combat that performed a combat action (Attack or Block) count as having survived until the end of the round. The Initiative player receives priority. When both pass, perform an INI Check for the end of the round: the controller of the highest-INI Character receives Initiative. Proceed to the End Phase.

title: End Phase
body:
Both players may play Spells and Trainings from hand at the end of the round. The phase has three steps.

Step 1 — At the end of the round
Trigger end-of-round abilities. Put the Initiative player's abilities on the Reaction Chain first, then the other player's. The Initiative player receives priority. When both pass with an empty chain, proceed to step 2.

Step 2 — Discard
Starting with the Initiative player, both players discard to the maximum hand size of eight. Resolve resulting triggers and repeat step 2. For simultaneous triggers, the Initiative player's go on the chain first. No player receives priority. Then proceed to step 3.

Step 3 — Round transition
All “until end of round” effects end. No player receives priority. If Characters die or abilities trigger as a result, resolve those effects and repeat step 2. Order simultaneous triggers by putting the Initiative player's effects on first. Finally, all remaining ASP expire. Proceed to the next round's Start Phase.

title: Priority and the Reaction Chain
body: The Reaction Chain establishes a clear order for resolving cards, abilities and their effects. The priority system determines who may actively add something to it.
html: The Reaction Chain establishes a clear order for resolving cards, abilities and their effects. The priority system determines who may actively add something to it.

title: Priority
body:
The player with priority may play cards or activate abilities and keeps priority until they choose to pass. When both players pass consecutively, resolve the most recently added card or ability. Priority then returns to the player who first receives it in the current phase:
- Main Phase 1: the player with Initiative.
- Main Phase 2: the player without Initiative.
- Combat Phase: the acting Character's controller.
- End Phase: the player with Initiative.
If both pass with an empty chain, advance to the next step. If it was the last step of a phase, advance to the next phase.

The chain resolves last in, first out. It is part of the game, not the battlefield (section 2.3). Played cards move from their previous location, such as the hand, onto the chain, then to their destination after resolving. They are no longer in their previous location once played.
Activated and triggered abilities on the chain are independent of their source. They remain and resolve even if that source leaves play or changes zones.

title: Game actions and card rules
body:
Playing cards and activating abilities require priority. Cards from hand must also obey their card type's timing restrictions (section 3.1):
- Characters, Artifacts, Rituals: only during your own turn.
- Trainings and Spells: during your own turn and at the end of the round.
- Resources: only as a special action during your own turn with an empty Reaction Chain.
Activated abilities may have restrictions stated in their card text. Otherwise they have no additional timing restrictions.

title: Playing a card
body:
Playing a card usually requires paying its printed ASP cost at the top left, and may require additional costs. If timing and priority permit playing it, use this order:
1. Announce the card from hand.
2. Choose a face-down mode if available, such as Hideout or another face-down method.
3. Put the card in the next unoccupied position on the Reaction Chain, face down if such a mode was chosen, otherwise face up. It is now an object on the chain, no longer a hand card.
4. Choose other modes, including Rise and any required effect modes.
5. Determine all targets: the destination slot for a permanent and all required “choose”/“target” choices.
6. Determine total costs. Apply, in order: ASP increases (including the Sovereign's off-colour surcharge); ASP reductions; effects setting minimum ASP costs; effects setting total ASP costs; additional-cost increases; additional-cost reductions; effects setting minimum additional costs; effects setting additional costs.
7. Pay total costs: deduct ASP from the reserve, then pay non-ASP additional costs such as life, discards or sacrifices.

Abilities triggered during this process wait until the card has been fully played. Then place the active player's triggers on the chain, followed by the inactive player's. The player who played the card retains priority.
An incorrectly played card, for example with an illegal target or insufficient resources, is an illegal action. Abort and reverse the process (chapter 14).

title: Activating and triggering abilities
body:
Abilities can be activated or triggered only while their source card is in play, unless the ability or another rule states otherwise. Abilities enter the Reaction Chain either through activation, with activation costs paid, or automatically when a triggering event occurs.
For both types, determine and lock in all relevant values, decisions and references when the ability is activated or triggers. Later changes to the source or reference values do not affect resolution unless the text explicitly says otherwise, such as “as this resolves”.

Activated abilities
These always have the form “[cost]: effect”. Wording such as “activate only if…”, “activate only once per round…” or “activate only as long as…” adds activation requirements. If a requirement is not met, activation is not allowed.
The player must have priority and control the card. Then:
1. Announce the ability.
2. Put it in the next unoccupied chain position, fixing its position.
3. Choose any required effect modes.
4. Announce all required “choose”/“target” choices.
5. Determine total costs in this order: ASP increases; ASP reductions; minimum ASP costs; total ASP costs; additional-cost increases; additional-cost reductions; minimum additional costs; fixed additional costs.
6. Pay ASP costs from the reserve, then non-ASP costs such as turning, life, discards or sacrifices.
Triggers caused during activation wait until it is complete, then go on the chain in active-player, inactive-player order. The activating player keeps priority.
Illegal activation, including an illegal target, insufficient resources or illegal timing, is aborted and reversed (chapter 14).

Triggered abilities
They trigger automatically when their event occurs, signalled by wording such as “when”, “whenever” or “at the beginning/end of…”. Triggering does not require priority.
Put triggered abilities on the chain once their triggering event is fully complete. For simultaneous triggers, first place the abilities of the player who first receives priority in the current phase, then the other player's. Each player orders their own simultaneous abilities.

Abilities triggered by zone changes
For abilities that refer to leaving a zone, check the affected object’s characteristics immediately before the zone change. For abilities that refer to entering a zone, check the new object’s characteristics immediately after the zone change.

Delayed triggered abilities
Effects may create abilities that wait for a specified future event. Until triggering, they have no independent card or zone relationship. Define their specified values, conditions and references when they are created. When their event occurs, put them on the chain and resolve them like other triggered abilities.

Targets and modes
The controller of the source chooses required targets and modes when putting a trigger on the chain. All targets must be legal then. After all triggers have been placed, assign priority according to the phase (section 3.1) and resolve abilities under the normal chain and resolution rules (section 4.3).

title: Resolving a card or ability
body:
When both players pass consecutively, resolve the top card or ability on the chain, last in, first out. Follow its rules text in order.
A permanent moves to its designated battlefield position if available; otherwise it goes to the Graveyard. A Spell goes to the Graveyard. An ability does not change zones; it ceases to exist after resolving. Then assign priority under section 3.2.1.
If all of a card or ability's selected targets have become illegal, for example through a zone change, it has no effect. An ability then ceases to exist; a card moves from the chain to the Graveyard.

If an effect cannot be applied in full, carry out all parts that can still be applied and omit only those that cannot. For example, Magic Missle deals 2 DMG to up to two Characters. If two legal targets were chosen and one is sacrificed before resolution, the remaining target still takes 2 DMG; no additional 2 DMG can be dealt. If all selected targets are absent at resolution, the entire effect is cancelled (fizzles).

title: Applying replacement effects
body: Effects that replace an effect or event are replacement effects. They can be recognised by wording such as “If [old effect], [replacement effect] instead”. For example: “If this Character would take damage, put a POW/HP +1/+1 counter on it instead.” If several replacement effects apply to the same object at the same time, the controller of the affected object determines their application order.

title: Spellpower versus Resistance: RES Check
body:
If an effect from a source with Spellpower would affect a card with RES, perform a RES Check for each affected target at resolution.
If the source's Spellpower is at least the target's RES, the effect applies normally to that target. If RES exceeds Spellpower, the effect does not affect that target. Other targets and other parts of the effect remain unaffected unless they also require a RES Check.

title: Astral points
body:
Astral points (ASP) pay for effects and cards. Generated ASP are collected in the ASP reserve, an abstract area rather than a battlefield zone.
ASP are usually generated by abilities. These use the Reaction Chain, are not immediate, and can be responded to. Playing a card or activating an ability is a closed sequence (sections 4.1 and 4.2), so all required ASP must be generated and already in the reserve before starting.
ASP remain until the end of the round. All remaining ASP expire in step 3 of the End Phase (section 3.1.5).

title: Additional costs
body:
Additional costs are paid as part of playing a card or activating an effect. Like ASP payment, paying them does not use the Reaction Chain. Pay all additional costs in the order required by the card or effect.

The Sovereign's off-colour surcharge is an additional cost applied in step 6a of section 4.1.

### Common additional costs

#### Sacrifice a permanent

Only its controller may sacrifice it; move it from play to the Graveyard.

#### Discard cards

Discard only cards in your own hand, moving them to the Graveyard.

#### Remove counters

Remove the exact named counter type. Unless stated otherwise, a permanent referring to counters as a cost means counters on itself. For example, “Remove 1 Time Counter: Draw a card” on an Artifact cannot use another permanent's Time Counter.

#### Pay life

Subtract the amount directly from the Sovereign's current life points. This is not damage. The player must have enough life to pay the full cost.

#### Turn

Rotate an unturned card by 180 degrees. An already turned card cannot pay this cost.

#### Change zones

For example, return a permanent to hand or move a card from the Graveyard to the Banished area (section 4.8).

title: Special actions
body:
Special actions do not use the Reaction Chain. They happen immediately and cannot be interrupted or prevented by an opponent's response. They require priority.
1. Play a Resource: put a Resource from hand into an empty Resource slot, or replace one when levelling up. This is allowed only if that player has not already placed a Resource in a Resource slot this round, during their own Main Phase and with an empty chain.
2. Move: turn a Character and move it to its designated new slot, for example from the Safety Zone to the War Zone. The Character must be unturned with INI greater than 0, and it must be the moving player’s Main Phase with that player holding priority. Move uses an action for the round. During combat, only the acting Character may do this, and it must have an action remaining.

If an effect instructs a special action, all its restrictions, including timing and action use, still apply unless the effect states otherwise.
Example: “Move It!” says “Move target Character”. At resolution, that Character performs Move. The Spell's controller controls the movement and makes all its decisions. The Character turns, spends an action and may move only to a free slot in an adjacent row (War Zone, Back Row or Binding slot).

title: Characteristic determination system (EBS)
body:
Every card and game object has defined characteristics at all times. Determine them by applying characteristic layers 1–7 strictly in order.

## Layer 1 — Owner, identity and base characteristics

This layer establishes the object's fundamental identity and the characteristics it has as a physical object or copy, before other effects apply.

### 1. Owner

The owner is the player whose deck contained the physical card at game start. A token's owner is the player under whose control it was created.

*Ownership never changes.*

### 2. Base object

Start from the printed card or the token's creation definition.

#### Copy effects

Apply copy effects here, replacing the printed information with that of the copied object.

#### Face-down cards

A card played face down has no further characteristics in play. It is a permanent without other card types until turned face up. Its controller may look at its hidden side at any time, and any ability on it to turn it face up remains usable.

### 3. Establishing base characteristics

After applying any copy effects, this layer establishes:

- **Name:** the card's name.
- **Costs:** ASP and additional-cost symbols.
- **Card types:**
    - *Main type:* such as Character, Resource or Spell.
    - *Supertype:* such as Mythic, Epic, Fundamental, Martial or Advisor.
    - *Subtype:* such as Human/Undead.
- **Colour identity:** indicated by the card's frame.
- **Rules text:** the text in the rules box.
- **Base numerical values:** printed POW, HP, RES, INI and Spellpower.

## Layer 2 — Control

By default, the controller is the player who put the card into play. Apply control-changing effects here.

## Layer 3 — Text and name

Start with layer 1's text and name, then apply effects changing them.

## Layer 4 — Type and colour

Start with layer 1's types and colours, then apply effects changing or adding them. Effects saying a card ‘becomes’ a type add that type to its existing types. A type is lost only if the rules text expressly says so.

## Layer 5 — Abilities

Start with the abilities in the rules text after layer 3. Apply ability-granting and ability-removing effects here.

## Layer 6 — Setting base values

Start with the printed numerical values from layer 1. Effects setting POW/HP, RES, INI or Spellpower to a specific value overwrite that value as the base for the next layer.

## Layer 7 — Modified values

Apply changes to the layer 6 base in this order:

1. Multipliers.
2. Additive modifiers.
3. Subtractive modifiers.
4. Exchanges of values, such as swapping POW and RES.

## Timestamp order

If two effects conflict within one layer, the newer timestamp wins: the effect that entered play or was activated later.

## Restrictions on actions

For conflicting permissions and prohibitions on actions such as playing, activating, attacking or moving, “can't” overrides “can”.

*Example: a Character required to attack each combat if able cannot attack if a Training says it cannot attack.*

body: This chapter defines card status by location under chapter 2 and the mechanical consequences of changing location.

  2. Reaction Chain: a temporary area for played cards and effects.
  3. ASP reserve: an abstract counter for available astral points.

title: Zone changes and resetting
body:
Moving between zone categories, such as from an active zone to an inactive area or from hand into play, makes a card a new object.
- Reset: the new object has no connection to the previous one. Remove all counters and damage counters; temporary and static effects end. Existing or future references to the old object become invalid unless the zone-changing effect explicitly provides otherwise.
- Tokens: tokens exist only in active zones. As soon as a token leaves an active zone, it ceases to exist in the other zone.
- Trainings: when an attached card changes zones, its Training stays behind unattached. It does not follow and goes to the Graveyard through a Gamestate Check (section 4.10).
- If a permanent changes zones due to a return effect, it can only be placed in a zone or slot controlled by its owner.

title: Definitions of values
body: Bluthelden® distinguishes base values, modified values and current values to resolve situations unambiguously.

title: Base value
body:
The base value is the starting point for calculation: printed POW, HP, RES, INI, Spellpower, LP or cost. Outside play, including Graveyard, hand, deck and Banished area, only base values exist; ignore modifications.
An effect that sets a value, such as “becomes 3/3”, temporarily sets a new base for the object in play (layer 6 in section 4.7).

If a printed value contains a variable, such as *, treat the variable as 0 when the card is outside play. In play, use the determined variable value as its base value or part of it.

title: Modified value
body: The modified value is the numerical maximum a Character can reach from its values and modifiers. Apply all permanent and temporary bonuses, penalties and multipliers through EBS layers 1–7. It caps healing (Regeneration) and is the basis for the current value.

title: Current value
body:
The current value describes the actual state of an object in play. Card or effect references to a number, such as “destroy a Character with HP 2 or less”, use the current value.

A)

**Current HP** = modified HP − accumulated damage. At 0 or less, the Character is destroyed by a Gamestate Check (section 4.10).

**Current life points** = modified life points − accumulated life loss. Accumulated life loss includes all life paid or otherwise lost and all damage taken. Life regeneration reduces accumulated life loss.

B)

**Current POW, RES and INI** normally equal their modified values.

Exception: turned RES and INI

- **System checks:** when checking action requirements (Attack, Block, Move) or automatic comparisons (INI Check, Spellpower/RES Check such as attaching Training), treat current INI and RES as 0.
- **Card references:** when a card or ability asks for a value, including target selection or exchanging RES and POW, the current value remains the modified value even while the Character is turned.

For queries, treat a negative current value as 0. Modifier calculations still use the actual value. *Example: RES 1 with two RES−1 counters is −1, but all RES comparisons treat it as 0. If the Character in the example temporarily gains +2 RES, its current RES is 1: the actual −1 plus 2.*

title: Gamestate Check (GSC)
body:
A GSC automatically corrects illegal game states. It does not use the Reaction Chain and cannot be interrupted.

## 1. When to check

Perform a GSC:

- After resolving an effect on the Reaction Chain.
- Immediately **before** a player would receive priority.
- Between the First Damage and normal combat damage segments.

## 2. Check procedure

Check and correct the following in order. Repeat the GSC if corrections create new states, for example death triggers, before granting priority:

1. **Sovereign at 0 or less life:** its controller loses. If both are affected simultaneously, the game is a draw.
2. **Empty-deck draw:** a player required to draw from an empty Pool or Spell Deck loses. If both are affected simultaneously, the game is a draw.
3. **Lethal damage:** destroy Characters with current HP of 0 or less and put them in the Graveyard.
4. Tokens outside active zones, for example in hand or Graveyard, cease to exist.
5. **Epic:** if a player controls multiple same-name Epic permanents in one Lane, they choose one and sacrifice the others.
6. **Mythic:** if a player controls multiple same-name Mythic permanents anywhere on the battlefield, they choose one and sacrifice the others.
7. **Unattached Training:** put a Training in play that is not attached to another permanent in the Graveyard.
8. **No slot:** a permanent that cannot be legally placed because no free slot is available goes to its owner's Graveyard instead.

title: Special combat mechanics
body: The structure of combat, Initiative, basic attacking and blocking are in section 3.1.4. Special actions, particularly Move, are in section 4.6. This chapter covers modifications to normal combat.

title: Attack variants
body:
This section explains modifications to the standard Attack combat action.

## Ranged Combat

From the Back Row, a Character with this ability may attack a Character in the same Lane's War Zone. This counts as an Attack combat action and uses **one action** for the round. It does not cause a Block reaction, so the attacked Character is not turned and does not lose an action. Ranged Combat is an attack-declaration modification, not an activated ability or targeting; Untargetable and Spectral Ward do not prevent it.

## Targeted Strike

When declaring an attack, choose the opposing Sovereign or a Character in the opposing War Zone of the same Lane. A chosen Character is forced to block even without a remaining Block action. If available, consume its action and turn it as for a normal block. This modifies attack declaration; it is not a triggered ability and is not prevented by targeting protection such as Untargetable or Spectral Ward.

## Two-Handed Combat

The Character has **two actions** per round instead of one. When choosing Attack, declare one or two attacks. Two attacks consume both available actions. The opponent may declare a separate Block reaction for each, if they have enough eligible Characters. Damage from all those attack actions is assigned simultaneously.

**Example:** *A 3/3 Character declares two attacks. The opponent has one eligible 2/2 blocker, which blocks the first attack. The second attack remains unblocked.*

***Damage result***

1. *The blocker takes 3 damage from the attacker's POW.*
2. *The opposing Sovereign takes 3 damage from the unblocked attack.*
3. *The attacker takes 2 damage from the blocker's POW.*

title: Block variants
body:
Normal blockers must be in the same War Zone, unturned and have an action remaining (section 3.1.4). These abilities modify that:
1. Flying: only Characters with Flying or Skyguard may block a Flying attacker.
2. Unblockable: the Character cannot be blocked; its attack does not allow a legal Block reaction.
3. Barrier: it takes no slot but belongs to its War Zone. If it is its player's only Character in that War Zone, all attacking Characters gain Targeted Strike with the Barrier automatically chosen as the attacked Character.

title: Advanced damage resolution
body:
Damage is normally simultaneous. These abilities modify it:

1. **First Damage**

    Add a First Damage segment:

    - *First Damage segment:* only Characters with First Damage deal damage. Perform a GSC before the normal segment (section 4.10).
    - *Normal segment:* surviving Characters that did not deal First Damage deal their damage.

2. **Punch**

    If combat damage to a blocker exceeds that blocker's **current HP**, deal the excess to the opposing Sovereign instead. Attacker and blocker must be in the same War Zone at damage resolution. If the blocker was removed beforehand, use 0 for its current HP.

*Calculation:* Damage to Sovereign = attacker's POW − blocker's current HP.

title: Determining affected cards
body:
When an effect refers to cards without “target” or “choose”, and no deterministic rule identifies them, its controller determines the affected cards when applying the effect.
This is not targeting, does not trigger abilities triggered by targeting, and is not affected by selection-restricting effects.
Example: a Spell with Spellpower 4 says “Return a Character to its owner's hand”. The opponent controls two Untargetable Characters, A with RES 3 and B with RES 5. Either can be selected despite Untargetable, but a RES Check still applies. A returns to its owner's hand; choosing B produces no effect because RES 5 exceeds Spellpower 4.

title: Conditions
body:
Conditions are binary keyword mechanics created by effects. A card either has a condition or does not; it cannot have multiple instances of the same condition. Condition counters or keyword abilities may grant them, but multiple sources still create only one instance of the condition.

title: Purpose and scope
body:
This rulebook governs Bluthelden® tournaments and supplements the game rules with organisational, formal and procedural provisions for competitive play. It aims to ensure a fair, consistent and understandable tournament process, comparable conditions for all participants, and clearly defined violations and consequences.
It applies to sanctioned events explicitly designated as such by tournament management. For unsanctioned games, demonstrations or private events, it applies only as agreed by organisers or players.
It does not replace the game rules. Game mechanics, card effects, timing and definitions follow the game rules and binding card text. House rules, alternative formats and simplified rules are not permitted in sanctioned tournaments.

title: Binding rules and hierarchy
body:
Apply the following order:

1. **Card text:** rules text published in the official Bluthelden [card database](https://octenarius.com) is binding and overrides general descriptions and differing printed text.
2. **Game rules:** govern mechanics, definitions, timing and interactions.
3. **Tournament rules:** govern organisation, procedures, responsibilities, violations and their treatment.
4. **Tournament management and Judge decisions:** binding during the tournament to interpret and enforce existing rules and preserve integrity.

If interpretations conflict during an event, tournament management's decision governs that event, even if later corrected or clarified.

title: Rule Enforcement Level (REL)
body:
REL describes the intended strictness, organisation and enforcement. It affects:

- Expected rules knowledge.
- Treatment of violations.
- The type and severity of measures and penalties.
- Interpretation of corrections.

Management announces the level and its application before the tournament.

In general:

- Lower levels prioritise smooth play and the player experience.
- Higher levels prioritise compliance, competitive integrity and consistent enforcement.

Deliberate violations, deception and unsporting conduct are unacceptable at every level.

The four levels are:

- REL 0 — Casual Play (unsanctioned).
- REL 1 — Basic Play.
- REL 2 — Advanced Play.
- REL 3 — Competitive Play.

title: Tournament software and result reporting
body:
Sanctioned Bluthelden® events must be run and evaluated using the official tournament software. This is a condition of sanctioning.

The software is used for:

- Managing players, rounds and pairings.
- Recording and evaluating match results.
- Documenting the event consistently.
- Official reporting and archiving.

An event not run or correctly reported through that software is unsanctioned and counts as Casual Play, regardless of how it is described publicly.
Management is responsible for correct use and complete, accurate reporting. Players must cooperate, particularly in confirming results and correctly identifying matches. 

Information, versions and access conditions are available at [www.bluthelden.net](https://www.bluthelden.net).

body:

body:
A Judge intervenes when a player asks a rules question, the game state is unclear, a violation is suspected or match-related tournament operation is disrupted. The Judge establishes the facts, rules, and directs continuation.

title: Tokens, counters and other aids
body:

title: Deck construction and legality

title: Definitions
body:
A game is one self-contained Bluthelden® game started, played and ended under the game rules.

A match is the smallest unit relevant to tournament scoring and normally consists of exactly one game.

A round is a tournament stage containing parallel matches. It ends when all its matches finish or are decided under the time rules.

title: Match formats
body:
Bluthelden® is designed for Best-of-One (BO1): one game determines the match. Deviations require explicit provision and organisational support by management.

As an optional exception, management may use Best-of-Three (BO3) for clearly defined stages. A match has up to three games and is won upon winning two.

BO3 takes substantially more time. Use it only where:

- No fixed time limit is needed, or
- Enough time is assured for all possible games.

Suitable examples include:

- Post-cut finals (Top 4/Top 8).
- Single-elimination events.
- Invitation-only events.
- Stages with particularly high competitive requirements.

BO3 is not recommended for ordinary rounds with strict time limits.

body:

title: End-of-time procedure

If no result is reached in the allotted time, grant two additional game rounds, beginning after the current game round. If there is still no winner, the game and normally the match are drawn. Both players must continue promptly without unnecessary delays.

title: General principles

title: Cheating potential and critical incidents
body:
An incident is critical only when it can distort competition one-sidedly or be deliberately exploited. The criteria are:
- It creates or could create a one-sided informational or decision advantage, or an illegal state enabling one.
- It could be used repeatedly or systematically as a strategy (cheating potential).
If these criteria are met, the Judge or management must record and forward the incident under chapter 15.

title: Game Rule Violation (GRV)
body:
A GRV is an unintentional misapplication of a game rule or illegal performance of a mandatory action when no more specific category applies.

Examples include:

- Incorrect action order.
- Incorrect timing, priority or response opportunities.
- Misapplied effects other than missed effects.
- Incorrect zone placement or placement in an inactive area.
- Incorrect conditions or counters.

GRVs often involve GSC timing and the Reaction Chain. Denying an opponent a legal response opportunity, practically or formally, can be a GRV.

Do not use this category when Hidden Information Error, Deck/Decklist Error, Unsporting Conduct or Cheating fits better.

body:

It includes:

- Time-based triggers.
- Mandatory ongoing conditions or degeneration.
- Other automatic or required processes.

The classification requires that:

- The effect is **mandatory**, not optional.
- Its condition has occurred.
- Its execution was omitted or attempted late enough to depart from the legal sequence.

Whether and how it can be resolved later follows chapter 14 and may depend on REL.

- Insults, aggression or intimidation.
- Deliberate distraction.
- Refusal to cooperate reasonably with officials.
- Abuse of processes such as Judge calls to disrupt or delay.

Avoidable slow play is also unsporting, particularly if it:

- Is repeated.
- Is used at decisive stages.
- Is recognisably intended to reach extra rounds.

- Manipulating hidden information.
- False statements to officials.
- Marking or manipulating cards, sleeves or decks.
- Other deception distorting competition.

body:

Measures serve to:

- Protect match and tournament integrity.

- Prevent cheating potential.
- Ensure consistent treatment of repeated or escalating incidents.

title: Application principles

Measures protect integrity and prevent repetition and cheating potential. They do not compensate for an in-game advantage and are not game corrections.

Apply them consistently, transparently and proportionately, considering extent, match and tournament impact, repetition, cooperation and cheating potential.

An error is not serious merely because it affects play; absence of intent does not automatically justify leniency. Objective harm to competition governs.

title: Available measures
body:
Measures may be used individually or in combination according to the incident, REL and overall context. Not all are penalties: advice, organisational interventions and time measures ensure proper operation. Scoring consequences apply when fair match integrity cannot otherwise be assured. Officials exercise discretion under section 13.1.

## (1) Caution

A non-punitive explanation of correct rules application, possibly identifying the relevant rule.

Appropriate for:

- First minor errors.
- Obvious misunderstandings without advantage potential.
- Learning or low-REL settings, particularly REL 0 or 1.

Normally not recorded across events, but management may make an internal record.

## (2) Warning

A documented formal measure indicating that the incident exceeds a simple misunderstanding or that repetition may escalate.

Appropriate when:

- Play or decisions were affected.
- The same or similar error repeats.
- A caution was already given.
- Greater care is expected, particularly at REL 2 or 3.

## (3) Upgrade / escalation

An increase in intervention because of repetition, severity or the overall situation, not an independent measure.

Relevant when:

- Errors repeat after cautions or warnings.
- Multiple similar errors occur.
- Repetition structurally distorts competition.
- Cheating potential increases.

Cautions can become Warnings, and Warnings can become scoring consequences. Disqualification is not automatic escalation; it must be justified by the overall severity and cheating potential.

## (4) Penalty

The affected Sovereign immediately loses **5 life points**. This may cause a game loss but does not automatically end the match.

Appropriate when more than a Warning is needed but Match Loss would be disproportionate, particularly for repeated errors or complex states with increased cheating potential.

At REL 1, use it only through the Caution → Warning → Penalty escalation. At REL 2 and above, it is a regular available measure. It is not intended at REL 0.

It may escalate to Match Loss.

## (5) Match Loss

The most severe regular scoring consequence within an ongoing match. Use when cautions, warnings, penalties or corrections cannot preserve fair competition, or continued violations require escalation.

Relevant to:

- Irreparable one-sided advantage.
- Inability to restore a legal state.
- Objective destruction of the basis of a fair match.

At REL 1 and above, it may follow Caution → Warning → Penalty → Match Loss after repeated opportunities to learn and correct.

At REL 2 and above, it may be immediate if the criteria are met, correction is impossible or insufficient and a Penalty would be inadequate.

## (6) Disqualification

The most severe tournament measure, particularly for Cheating, serious unsporting conduct, irreparable deck/list errors or excessive abuse potential.

It excludes the player from the current event regardless of previous results and must always be documented and forwarded under chapter 15.

Actual realised advantage is not required; attempts, knowing acceptance or planned exploitation may suffice. It is a last resort for substantial abuse potential, Cheating, or repeated unrepentant violations threatening integrity.

It applies only to participation in the sanctioned event.

Measures may be used individually or in combination according to the incident, REL and overall context. Not all are penalties: advice, organisational interventions and time measures ensure proper operation. Scoring consequences apply when fair match integrity cannot otherwise be assured. Officials exercise discretion under section 13.1.

(1) Caution

A non-punitive explanation of correct rules application, possibly identifying the relevant rule.

Appropriate for:

  • First minor errors.
  • Obvious misunderstandings without advantage potential.
  • Learning or low-REL settings, particularly REL 0 or 1.

Normally not recorded across events, but management may make an internal record.

(2) Warning

A documented formal measure indicating that the incident exceeds a simple misunderstanding or that repetition may escalate.

Appropriate when:

  • Play or decisions were affected.
  • The same or similar error repeats.
  • A caution was already given.
  • Greater care is expected, particularly at REL 2 or 3.

(3) Upgrade / escalation

An increase in intervention because of repetition, severity or the overall situation, not an independent measure.

Relevant when:

  • Errors repeat after cautions or warnings.
  • Multiple similar errors occur.
  • Repetition structurally distorts competition.
  • Cheating potential increases.

Cautions can become Warnings, and Warnings can become scoring consequences. Disqualification is not automatic escalation; it must be justified by the overall severity and cheating potential.

(4) Penalty

The affected Sovereign immediately loses 5 life points. This may cause a game loss but does not automatically end the match.

Appropriate when more than a Warning is needed but Match Loss would be disproportionate, particularly for repeated errors or complex states with increased cheating potential.

At REL 1, use it only through the Caution → Warning → Penalty escalation. At REL 2 and above, it is a regular available measure. It is not intended at REL 0.

It may escalate to Match Loss.

(5) Match Loss

The most severe regular scoring consequence within an ongoing match. Use when cautions, warnings, penalties or corrections cannot preserve fair competition, or continued violations require escalation.

Relevant to:

  • Irreparable one-sided advantage.
  • Inability to restore a legal state.
  • Objective destruction of the basis of a fair match.

At REL 1 and above, it may follow Caution → Warning → Penalty → Match Loss after repeated opportunities to learn and correct.

At REL 2 and above, it may be immediate if the criteria are met, correction is impossible or insufficient and a Penalty would be inadequate.

(6) Disqualification

The most severe tournament measure, particularly for Cheating, serious unsporting conduct, irreparable deck/list errors or excessive abuse potential.

It excludes the player from the current event regardless of previous results and must always be documented and forwarded under chapter 15.

Actual realised advantage is not required; attempts, knowing acceptance or planned exploitation may suffice. It is a last resort for substantial abuse potential, Cheating, or repeated unrepentant violations threatening integrity.

It applies only to participation in the sanctioned event.

Whether the player must leave the area or venue is separately determined by the organiser's venue rights, independently of the tournament classification.

title: Error correction
body: This chapter addresses game-state corrections only. Whether a measure under chapter 13 also applies is assessed independently. Restore a legal and fair state without creating new imbalance or informational advantage.

title: Correction principles
body:
The following principles apply to all corrections:

## Fairness before perfection

Aim for a fair, playable state, not a perfect reconstruction of a hypothetical legal sequence.

## Minimal intervention

Intervene as little as possible. The longer ago the error and the more later decisions, the more cautious a backup should be.

## No new informational advantage

Do not create additional information or allow retrospective decisions using knowledge unavailable in legal play.

## Pause immediately

Take no further actions until a Judge or management resolves the issue.

## Official decision

Corrections are ordered by a Judge or management. Players may correct only obvious, unambiguous errors with no hidden-information impact, by mutual agreement. At REL 2 and above, corrections should generally involve a Judge.

title: Procedure when an error is found
body:
When a possible violation is found:

1. **Pause play.**
2. **Establish facts.**
    - a) Which rules were violated?
    - b) When did the error occur?
    - c) Which cards, counters or zones are affected?
    - d) What happened before discovery?
3. **Determine effects.**
    - a) What part of the game state is illegal?
    - b) Were subsequent actions based on that illegal state?
4. **Choose a correction.**
    - a) If section 14.1 permits, back up to the last clearly legal state.
    - b) If reconstruction is impossible or unhelpful, correct only the present state if it is a GRV.
    - c) Resolve missed mandatory triggers if legally possible, fully and in the required order, without creating improper one-sided informational or decision advantages.
5. **Carry out the correction.**
6. **Establish an unambiguous state.**

Add time needed for a Judge's correction under section 10.4.1. The Judge determines the extent under section 14.1.

title: Backup
body:
A backup reverses actions to restore an earlier state.

## When a backup is allowed

It is allowed only when:

- The sequence is clearly reconstructable.
- Few later actions occurred.
- Hidden-information changes are absent or controllable.
- No new advantage results.

## Limits on backups

A backup is generally unsuitable after:

- Cards were drawn or searched for.
- Decks were shuffled or random effects performed.
- Multiple hidden-information decisions were made.
- The error was discovered late.

Prefer direct state correction in these cases.

title: Game Rule Violation (GRV)
body:
A Game Rule Violation occurs when game rules were applied incorrectly or an illegal game state arose.

Typical corrections:

- Incorrect markers, conditions or values:
    - Set, adjust or remove incorrect markers and conditions.
- Incorrect zone or Lane assignment:
    - Move misplaced cards to the correct zone or Lane.
    - Identify the correct active Lane.
- Misapplied modifiers:
    - Determine current values correctly. Existing damage remains unless safe reconstruction is possible.
- Reversing an incorrect play:
    - Reverse an incorrect play with no further consequences, for example playing a level 2 Character with only a level 1 Resource.

Prefer direct correction over a backup when no hidden-information intervention is required.

title: Missed mandatory effects
body:
Mandatory effects, such as degenerative conditions, offer no choice whether to trigger. Correction depends particularly on how much time has passed.

## Prompt discovery

When discovered promptly, normally in the same round, resolve the effect later if execution is clearly reconstructable. If required decisions about modes, targets or order can be made legally without affecting the game state, assume they were made accordingly.

## Late discovery

Do not completely replay the effect retrospectively. Resume legal play at the next possible correct point.

## Principle

A correction must not allow decisions to be remade or changed using newly learned information.

title: Hidden Information Errors
body:
Information already gained cannot be undone. Reduce asymmetry and restore randomness where possible instead of pretending to erase knowledge.

## Correction guidelines

### Accidentally viewing hidden cards

After accidentally viewing cards, do not give that player new decisions about selecting, ordering or replacing those cards unless such a choice was already legal. Where possible, randomise the affected hidden area so knowledge does not create an additional structural advantage.

### Typical cases and fixes

#### A) Accidentally seeing deck contents

If one card is seen and the deck is otherwise random with no known order information, shuffle the deck and offer the opponent a cut.
If shuffling would erase legally known information, such as a known bottom card or a card placed at a defined position, do not automatically randomise. Stabilise the state without creating new choices; the Judge decides under section 14.1.

#### B) Drawing too many cards

If the extra cards can be unambiguously identified, return them to the correct zone. If their original deck position cannot be determined, shuffle the deck and offer a cut.
If extra cards cannot be identified, do not back up. Correct only as far as possible without further asymmetry, for example by restoring the proper hand size through random selection. Exercise particular care because of the high abuse potential.

#### C) Incorrectly revealing hand cards

Correction is relevant only when revealing was based on an incorrect assumption that a rule or effect required it. 

- The information cannot be erased.
- Correct the assumption and continue legally.
- Reveal no additional cards and allow no additional decisions based on the disclosure.

Voluntary, deliberate or careless disclosure, such as dropped or accidentally visible cards, does not require a game correction. Continue unchanged.

title: Deck / Decklist Errors
body:
Deck / Decklist Errors concern tournament legality or consistency between a deck and its list.

## Principle

Keep the deck clearly legal throughout the event.

## Typical corrections

- Deck differs from list:
    - Adjust the deck to match, then randomise.
- Obvious writing or naming error:
    - Correction is allowed if the error is unambiguous. Classify the incident and determine any measure under chapters 12 and 13.
- Card in the wrong Pool or Spell Deck:
    - Move it correctly and randomise both decks.
- Marked or damaged sleeves or cards:
    - Replace or standardise sleeves, then randomise.
- Wrong card count despite agreement with the list:
    - Remove excess cards.
    - If short, add standard Resource cards usable in either deck, such as Priest or Smith.
- Illegal list under format, bans, size or rarity limits:
    - Compare with the actual deck and correct the list if the deck is legal.

At REL 2 and above, severity may justify Disqualification. Investigate carefully.

title: Purpose and scope
body: This chapter governs appeals, records of tournament incidents and investigations of suspected Cheating. It supplements chapter 12 categories, chapter 13 measures and chapter 14 corrections with procedures, particularly rights and duties when integrity may be affected beyond the immediate game situation.

title: Appeals
body:
Only a directly affected player in the match may appeal a Judge's rules or procedural decision. Spectators and players in other matches may not.
Appeals may challenge interpretation, infraction classification under chapter 12 or measures under chapter 13. Purely organisational decisions affecting everyone equally, such as timing, seating, pairings and round operation, are not appealable.

title: Appeal procedure
body:
Appeal immediately after the decision is announced, verbally to the Judge who made it. The Judge forwards it to the appeal authority.
Pause the match during the appeal and add the time under section 10.4.1.

title: Appeal authority
body:
At REL 2 and above, appoint a Head Judge, the highest rules authority, who hears appeals against other Judges. The Head Judge may also observe matches and make rulings directly. Their decisions cannot be further appealed.
At REL 0 or 1, management acts as the final appeal authority unless a Head Judge is appointed.
The appeal authority reviews independently, is not bound by the initial assessment, and may confirm, modify or overturn it.

The appeal authority reviews independently, is not bound by the initial assessment, and may confirm, modify or overturn it.

title: Effect and binding force
body:
An appeal does not suspend the original decision unless the appeal authority expressly orders a temporary suspension.
The appeal decision is final and binding for the event and cannot be appealed again. Implement resulting game consequences immediately where consistent with chapter 14.

title: Documentation requirements
body:
Management must document incidents to make decisions reviewable and support consistent application beyond a single event. Required records include:
- Warnings, Penalties, Match Losses and Disqualifications.
- Critical incidents under section 12.4.
- Appeals and outcomes under section 15.2.
- Every investigated Cheating suspicion, regardless of outcome.
At REL 0 or 1, records may be limited to Disqualifications, suspected Cheating and critical incidents. At REL 2 and above, all listed records are mandatory.

body:

body: Promptly send documented incidents to Bluthelden® Organized Play after the event, using the contact methods, such as email, specified by Organized Play.

title: Principle
body:
Protect tournament integrity and players against unjust accusations through a careful, fair process. Cheating findings are serious and may have far-reaching consequences.
All elements in section 12.5.6 must be present together: intent, a rules violation and an actual or attempted advantage.

title: Starting an investigation
body:
Investigate when a Judge, management or player raises a specific, reasoned suspicion of a deliberate violation under section 12.5.6.
A Judge or management investigates. At REL 2 and above, involve the Head Judge where possible. Immediately pause the match and add the investigation time to the round allowance. Both players must cooperate and answer truthfully.

title: Establishing facts and hearing players
body:
Establish events as fully as possible using objective evidence and statements. In particular:
- Interview players separately so neither hears or responds to the other's account.
- Preserve and inspect card positions, markers, conditions, life points and Graveyard contents.
- Examine decks, lists, sleeves and other materials where relevant.
- Interview uninvolved witnesses if available.
- Check records of similar incidents at this or other events.
Both players may fully present their perspective before a decision. Do not disclose hidden game information or improperly reveal the other player's account during questioning.

title: Assessment standard
body:
All three elements are required: a violation of card text or game/tournament rules; knowing, deliberate conduct or conscious acceptance of the violation; and an actual or attempted advantage for the player or disadvantage for the opponent.

The standard is clear conviction: the investigating authority must be highly confident from the evidence that all three are present. Mere suspicion, advantage alone or theoretical intent is insufficient.

Resolve doubt in the accused player's favour. If Cheating cannot be established with clear conviction, classify and handle the incident under the appropriate other category in chapter 12.

Officials must treat the accused fairly and respectfully. Suspicion is not prejudgment; preserve the benefit of doubt until a final finding.

title: Appendix I – Rules terminology
body:
Original appendix from the German tournament rulebook. The source wording is preserved; translated explanations are available in the glossary.

**Tabelle I.1: Übersicht Regelbegriffe**

| Begriff | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| **Abstrakte Spielbereiche** | Bereiche, die für das Spiel verwendet werden, aber nicht direkt auf dem Spielfeld abgebildet werden. Beispielsweise ASP- Vorrat und die Reaktionskette. |
| **Aktive Zonen** | Zonen, die sich auf dem phyischen Spielfeld befinden und in der Combat Zone, Safety Zone oder Regierungszone liegen. |
| **Aktivierte Fähigkeit** | Jeder durch einen Spieler mit Priorität durch Bezahlen von Kosten auslösbare Effekt. Immer erkennbar am Schema [Kosten]: [Effekt]. |
| **Aktueller Wert** | Statuswert, welcher durch vollständige Anwendung aller Modifikatoren resultiert. |
| **Angreifen/ Angriff** | Auswählbare Aktion in der Kampfphase für den handelnden Charakter. |
| **Artefakt** | Typ einer bleibenden Karte; in der Regierungszone zu platzieren im Feld für bleibende Karten |
| **ASP, ASP-Vorrat** | Abkürzung für Astralpunkte bzw. Astralpunkte Vorrat. |
| **Back-Row** | Bereich in der Safety Zone unmittelbar hinter den Slots der War Zone und über den Slots für Binding und Ressourcen. |
| **Banished Zone** | Ablageplatz für alle aus dem Spiel verbannten (banished) Karten. |
| **Beschwören (Summon) / Beschwörung (Summoning)** | Ausspielen einer bleibenden Karte aus der Hand, welche auf die Reaktionskette gelegt wird. |
| **Besitzer** | Der Besitzer einer Karte ist der Spieler, welcher die Karte zu Beginn des Spiels in seinem Deck hat. Bei Token ist der Spieler der Besitzer, bei dem der Token das Spielfeld betritt. Bei Fähigkeiten ist der Besitzer der Fähigkeit, der Spieler, der die Karte kontrolliert, welche die Fähigkeit auslöst. |
| **Binding Slot** | Slot in der Safety Zone, unter der Backrow und links neben dem Ressourcen-Slot. |
| **Bleibende Karte** | Jede Karte, welche einen Platz auf dem Spielfeld in den Aktiven Zonen einnehmen kann. |
| **Block / Blocken** | Kampfaktion, als Reaktion auf einen Angriff. |
| **Charakter** | Typ von bleibenden Karten, welche in der Slots für Charaktere platziert werden können. |
| **Dauerhafter Effekt** | Effekte die wirken, ohne aktiviert oder ausgelöst werden zu müssen. |
| **Degenerierende Effekt Counter** | Alle Marker, die einen Statuswert verringern oder einen Zustand gemäß Kapitel 6.2. verursachen und als „negativer Zustand“ gekennzeichnet sind. |
| **Fernkampf** | Angriff aus der Back-Row auf einen Charakter in der War Zone (Keyword: Ranged Combat). |
| **Friedhof** | Ablageort für zerstörte, geopferte oder abgeworfene Karten. |
| **Gamestate Check** | Automatische Prüfung des Spielzustandes und dessen Korrektur, bevor Spieler Priorität erhalten. |
| **Grundwert** | Aufgedruckte Werte auf der physischen Karten oder dessen Kopie. |
| **Hand (Handkarten)** | Blutheldenkarten die ein Spieler physisch in der Hand hält bzw. in der versteckten Zone "Hand" sich befinden. |
| **Herrscher** | Kartentyp, startet das Spiel im Herrscher Slot und bestimmt über die zulässigen Pool-Deck Karten und zusätzliche Ausspielkosten. |
| **Hitpoints (HP)** | Statuswert eines Charakters. Durch erlittenen Schaden wird der Wert reduziert um den gleichen Betrag. Sind die HP eines Charakters 0 oder niedriger, wird er zerstört und in den Friedhof gelegt. |
| **Inaktive Plätze** | Bereiche des Spielfeldes, welche nicht als "im Spiel" befindlich definiert sind. |
| **Initiative (INI)** | Statuswert eines Charakters. Wird für INI-Checks und Kampfreihenfolge benötigt. |
| **Interzonen- Bewegung** | Bewegung einer Karte zwischen verschiedenen Zonen innerhalb der Aktiven Zone. |
| **Kampfaktion** | In der Kampfphase wählbare Aktionen "Angriff" und "Block" sowie "Ranged Combat" sind Kampfaktionen. |
| **Kampfzone (Combat Zone)** | Summe aller Kriegszonen (War Zone). |
| **Kartentyp** | Regeltechnische Kategorie einer Karte, bestimmt über generelle Ausspielrestriktionen und Platzierungen auf dem Spielfeld. |
| **Kontrolle, kontrollierender Spieler** | Eigenschaft einer Karte, die bestimmt wer die Fähigkeiten und Entscheidungen für die die Kontrolle benötigt wird, durchführen darf. Festlegung gem. Eigenschaftsbestimmungssystem. |
| **Kriegszone (War Zone)** | Kombination der Front-Rows einer Lane (beider Spieler). |
| **Lane** | Kombination aller Plätze der Safety Zone bis Front-Row beider Spieler, begrenzt durch das Spielfeld anhand durchgezogener Linien. Eine Lane umfasst eine Breite von zwei Slots. |
| **Lebenspunkte (LP)** | Statuswert eines Herrschers. Wird durch erlittenen Schaden reduziert um den gleichen Betrag. Fällt die LP eines Herrschers auf 0 verliert der Spieler des Herrschers das Spiel. |
| **Magiewert / Spellpower** | Statuswert auf Karten. Wird für den Systemabgleich zwischen Magiewert und Resistenz verwendet, um zu ermitteln ob ein Karteneffekt eintritt. |
| **Modifizierter Wert** | Resultierender Wert für einen Statuswert, nach Anwendung aller Modifkatoren. |
| **Nicht bleibende Karte** | Karten, die aufgrund ihres Kartentyps nicht auf dem Spielfeld in einer aktiven Zone platziert werden können. |
| **Opfern** | Eine Karte kann durch einen Effekt oder zum Bezahlen von Kosten geopfert werden. Es kann dabei nur eine Karte geopfert werden, welche zum Zeitpunkt des Bezahlens oder des verrechnen des Effekts durch den Spieler, der das Opfer erbringen muss, kontrolliert wird. Es ist dazu nicht erforderlich, dass diese Karte physisch auf der eigenen Spielfeldhälfte liegt. Opfern bedeutet, dass die Karte aus dem Spiel direkt in den Friedhof gelegt wird. Es stellt mechanistisch nur einen Zonenwechsel dar, ist also kein „Zerstöreffekt“. Die Auswahl eines Opfers erfolgt durch den Spieler, der die Kosten zu Bezahlen hat oder der Ziel von einem Effekt, der ihn zum opfern zwingt, wird. |
| **Pool, Pool-Deck** | Verdeckter Kartenstapel, der Karten mit dem Poolsymbol enthält. |
| **Power (POW)** | Statuswert eines Charakters. Der POW Wert gibt den Schaden an, den ein Charakter im Kampf verursacht. |
| **Priorität** | Regeltechnischer Status eines Spielers (mit oder ohne Priorität). Zum Ausspielen von Karten oder Aktivieren von Fähigkeiten wird die Priorität benötigt. |
| **Reaktionskette (Reaction Chain)** | Abstrakter Spielbereich, auf den alle ausgespielten Karten und aktivierten sowie ausgelösten Fähigkeiten gelegt werden, bevor diese das Spiel betreten oder verrechnet werden. |
| **Regierungszone** | Sammlung der Slots für die Herrscherkarte, die Rune sowie bleibende Karten, die keine Charaktere sind. |
| **Resistenz (RES)** | Statuswert eines Charakters, wird zum Vergleich zwischen Magiewert und RES herangezogen, um die Wirksamkeit von Effekten zu bestimmen. |
| **Ressource** | Kartentyp, kann nur in einem Resourcen-Slot platziert werden. Hiervon ausgenommen ist die Rune, welche nur im Runen-Slot platziert werden darf. |
| **Ritual** | Kartentyp, wird im Slot für bleibende Karten platziert. |
| **Rune** | Kartentyp, wird im Rune-Slot zu Beginn des Spiels platziert. |
| **Schaden (DMG)** | Regeleffekt, der die LP oder HP um den gleichen Betrag senken. Wird akkumuliert auf Charakteren gezählt. |
| **Sicherheitszone (Safety Zone)** | Bereich des Spielfeldes oberhalb der Regierungszone und unterhalb der Front-Row |
| **Spell-Deck** | Kartenstapel der verdeckt auf dem Platz für das Spell-Deck gelegt wird. |
| **Sterben** | Sterben bezeichnet den Zonenwechsel eines Charakters aus dem Spiel in den Friedhof. Dies kann durch das Erreichen von 0 HP oder auch durch direkte Effekte erfolgen. Jeder Charakter der diesen Zonenwechsel vollzieht, gilt als „gestorben“. |
| **Token** | Durch einen Spieleffekt erzeugte bleibende Karten. Eigenschaften und Art des Tokens werden durch den erzeugenden Effekt bestimmt. |
| **Training** | Kartentyp, wird an andere bleibende Karten angelegt und nimmt keinen Slot auf dem Spielfeld ein. |
| **Werte** | Statuswerte auf einer Karte (z.B. RES, INI, POW/HP, Magiewert, Spellpower) |
| **Wirken (Cast)** | Ausspielen einer nicht bleibenden Karte aus der Hand auf die Reaktionskette. |
| **Zauberspruch/Spell** | Kartentyp, nicht bleibende Karte. |
| **Zonenwechsel** | Wechsel der Position einer bleibenden Karte aus der aktiven Zone in einen inaktiven Platz oder Bereich außerhalb des Spielfeldes. |
